stale/draws: The policy gradient learns from the model's own draws. Draw ten answers from the seven times eight model, and each turns up about as often as its probability: fifty six comes up five times, fifty four three times, and sixty four twice.
stale/slow: Drawing long answers is slow, so take several gradient steps on the same batch. Each step is an update.
stale/old: Call the model that drew the batch pi old. It stays fixed, while the model being trained, pi, moves with every update.
stale/moved: Say one update leaves pi at zero point six, zero point three and zero point one. Drawn fresh from pi, fifty six would come up six times in ten, and sixty four once.
stale/stale: But this batch still holds five and two: it counts answers as pi old drew them.
ratio/fix: So weigh each draw by how much more pi likes it than pi old did: pi over pi old.
ratio/w56: Fifty six had zero point five, and now has zero point six. zero point six over zero point five is one point two.
ratio/six: So its five draws count as six, just as in a fresh batch.
ratio/w64: Sixty four had zero point two, and now has zero point one, so each draw counts a half, and its two count as one. Fifty four kept zero point three, and counts once.
ratio/rho: This weight is the probability ratio, written with the Greek letter rho. Before any update, pi is pi old, and every ratio is one.
ratio/kahn: Weighing draws like this is called importance sampling. Herman Kahn and Andrew Marshall described it in 1953, to make simulations cheaper.
ratio/schulman: In 2015, John Schulman and colleagues used this ratio to train policies on draws from an older policy.
ratio/next: When the updates are done, the trained model draws the next batch, and becomes the new pi old.
objective/J: As in the log trick, training raises J, the expected reward. With fifty six marked one and the rest zero, J is just the probability of fifty six.
objective/plain: The batch's plain average reward is five in ten, zero point five: the J of pi old, not of pi.
objective/weighted: Weigh each reward by its ratio, and five draws counting one point two each, over ten, make zero point six: the J of pi.
objective/obj: What training raises is called its objective. Here it is the batch's average of the ratio times the advantage, A, used in place of the reward as before.
objective/term: With a baseline of zero point five, fifty six has an advantage of zero point five, so its term is one point two times zero point five: zero point six.
objective/push: The others have an advantage of minus zero point five. Raising the objective pushes fifty six up and the other two down: A sets the direction, and the ratio how much each draw counts.
logs/tiny: A real answer is many tokens long, and its probability is theirs multiplied together: twenty tokens at a half each make less than one in a million.
logs/logs: So code adds up their logs instead. Say an answer had ln pi old of minus twelve point four, and now has ln pi of minus twelve point seven.
logs/quot: The log of a quotient is the top's log minus the bottom's. So ln rho is minus twelve point seven, minus minus twelve point four: minus zero point three.
logs/exp: Then rho is e to the minus zero point three: about zero point seven four. Below one, so this answer became less likely.
logs/token: A single token's ratio works the same way: its new probability over its old one.
